lead.title: Ed Miliband defends doing 2015 election interview with Russell Brand, saying he was ‘taking him on’ not endorsing him – UK politics live
lead.summary: Ed Balls, shadow chancellor at the time, said he had warned Labour leader not to go ahead with ‘ridiculous’ interview Good morning. There are two issues that will dominate the political news this week – the EU reset, and the Alan Milburn report on youth unemployment – and this morning there are new lines on both of these issues. Andy Burnham has set out “three tests” for the deal that he is due to agree with the EU at a summit on Friday. Tonight he is giving the traditional prime ministerial speech to the lord mayor’s banquet in London, which by convention focuses on foreign policy, and, according to the overnight briefing from Downing Street, he will announce three tests. No 10 says: Ahead of this week’s UK-EU Summit, the prime minister will set out three tests for any agreement: -First, it must be consistent with the manifesto and the government’s red lines. It’s like the Emperor’s new clothes – where no one is prepared to say the obvious truth. Well, I say it as I see it. And to be frank, the Emperor has nothing on. The Brexit we were given has not worked. We have lost more than we gained. Alan Milburn is expected to say that employer national insurance for workers under the age of 25 should be cut in his report published tomorrow, the BBC is reporting. Many of Milburn’s recommendations have already been made public, but this is new, and it is likely to be welcomed by Kemi Badenoch, who is holding a press conference later, because the Tories have repeatedly been saying that Rachel Reeves’s decision to raise employer national insurance has been bad for jobs. top.title: Delaware hit by rare November tornado
top.summary: Meanwhile, severe thunderstorms bring hailstones the size of baseballs in Argentina The National Weather Service in the US has confirmed that an EF1 tornado touched down south-east of Newark in the Salem Woods neighbourhood, Delaware, on Thursday. The tornado reached 160 metres wide, had a path length of 4.4 miles (7.1km) and reached estimated peak winds of up to 100mph (161km/h). There were no injuries or fatalities but windows and roofs were damaged on several homes, a large hotel sign fell on to a number of cars, and a semi truck overturned on I95. Although Delaware often experiences a few tornadoes every year, this is only the second time the state has had tornado activity in November since 1950, according to the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration. The only other November tornado recorded was in 1989. Severe storms have also resulted in tornadoes in Argentina as well as large hailstones. A round of severe thunderstorms moved through the central Córdoba province on Friday, bringing hailstones up to the size of a baseball (about 7.5cm in diameter). Parts of the province recorded up to 73mm of rainfall in just six hours early on Saturday. Such storms are common at this time of year. Water vapour from the Amazon meeting the Andes quickly condenses, resulting in massive cloud formations often associated with heavy downpours, lightning, tornadoes and large hailstones. Culture.title: Not All Those Who Wander Are Lost album review – Anna Lapwood
Culture.summary: Lapwood/Nidaros Cathedral Girls’ Choir (Sony) Lapwood’s arrangements of Howard Shore’s film score are in gothic overdrive played on Trondheim’s Nidaros Cathedral organ, while her Elvish additions and an ethereal choir shine When a fan requested she play Concerning Hobbits from The Lord of the Rings, little did Anna Lapwood imagine that she would go on to spend a year turning Howard Shore’s leitmotif-led soundtrack into a full-blown organ symphony. Remarkably, she transcribed all but one segment by ear, a feat in itself. That she manages to tell the story chronologically over a 38-minute, three-movement span is equally impressive. But wait, there’s more. Reckoning the symphony would benefit from the human voice, she incorporated a handful of songs, performing them live – in Tolkien’s Elvish dialect – while playing the Nidaros Cathedral organ in Trondheim, Norway. The results are frequently convincing, though the folksy music of the Shire is less effective on the organ than the baleful music of Sauron and the Ringwraiths. The latter in particular captures the sounds we associate with Widor, Boëllmann and Vierne in full gothic overdrive. If anything, Lapwood could afford to let rip more often, though her finger- and foot-work shine, as do the ethereal voices of the Nidaros Cathedral Girls’ Choir. Continue reading...

Culture.title: ‘I have to sell my bum on OnlyFans to go on tour’: Kate Nash on fame, feminism and fighting the music business
Culture.summary: She threw a (metaphorical) brick through Spotify’s window and exposed industry failings with her ‘Butts for Tour Buses’ campaign. Now the singer is embracing her Irish roots with her new album’s fighting spirit Kate Nash was standing on a fire truck in a showgirl outfit complete with white tights and pink G-string, shouting through a loudhailer about the music industry’s failure to pay artists fairly, when she wondered if she’d gone too far. It was 2024 and the truck, which made pit stops outside the London offices of Spotify and Live Nation, had a large black-and-white picture of Nash’s bum on the back along with the words “Butts for Tour Buses” – a reference to her newly launched OnlyFans account, which she was using to fund her tour. That afternoon, she called her manager Kat. “I told her: ‘I’ve thrown a brick through the window at Spotify.’ She went: ‘What, literally?’ and I said: ‘No, but I’ve been standing outside their offices with a megaphone, so that relationship is over. I don’t think we’ll be making their New Music Friday feature.’ And we didn’t.” Continue reading...

Culture.title: The Sensualist by Gary Shteyngart review – a delectable romp through life’s pleasures
Culture.summary: From martinis to capybara videos, the novelist celebrates the little things (some more expensive than others) that bring him joy In 2024, the novelist Gary Shteyngart flew from New York to Milan in search of the perfect midnight-blue suit. There he chose fabric, before flying to Hong Kong to be fitted for four shirts, and on to Tokyo, where he was measured by master tailor Yuhei Yamamoto and master shoe­maker Yohei Fukuda. A short king (“five foot five and a half, with that ‘half’ doing a lot of work”), Shteyngart dreamed of a fit to disappear his 52-year-old moobs (“my tatas”, “my chimichangas”) and melt the heart of the toughest maitre d’ at the most in-demand restaurants. And guess what? The world’s finest craftsmen will give you all that – though Shteyngart, who emigrated from Leningrad to the US in 1979, argues that a great suit serves a deeper need than vanity. Trying it on two days after Trump’s second election, “it was the final certificate of naturalization … I couldn’t make my adopted country fall out of love with fascism, but at least I could enjoy my new shoes.” Clothes become an advanced form of self-care. Culture.title: The DCU’s James Gunn and Peter Safran are out – this is the biggest disaster to hit superhero movies in years
Culture.summary: The adventurous weirdness of the Gunn/Safran era that fans responded to is now history. Can the DCU ever get back on track? What was Warner Bros’ plan in 2022 , when the studio decided to reboot its superhero output, jettison the increasingly muddled DC Extended Universe (DCEU) and replace it with a sparkling new DC Universe (DCU)? In part it was to wipe the slate clean after years of false starts, abandoned storylines and tonal lurches. There was a little bit of Marvel envy to proceedings, and quite possibly a desire to avoid having to ever again discuss Batman v Superman: Dawn of Justice’s numerous failings . But mostly it was to take advantage of hiring of a man whom nobody could accuse of being short of ideas on how to make comic book movies. To a greater or lesser extent, the plan was James Gunn. Fast forward four years, and that plan lies in tatters. Gunn and his fellow DC Studios CEO Peter Safran have this week been fired (though they will reportedly stay on as film-makers), and Jeremy Latcham, another former Marvel man, is the new boss. What is the plan now? Nobody seems to know, and there is not much point asking David Ellison, the man whose Skydance empire has now gobbled up two of the former big five Hollywood studios (Paramount last year and Warner last month). That would be like asking for directions from a man who has just set fire to the map. Continue reading...
